title: torch.compile slower or failing for GNN training with NeighborLoader dynamic batches
body: My simple PyG GCN benchmark trains with NeighborLoader, so its mini-batches have dynamic shapes. Although PyG's simple gather/scatter compile tests pass with static and dynamic shapes, eager mode is faster than torch.compile on this benchmark, and the logs show TorchDynamo repeatedly reaching its cache-size limit because tensor sizes and strides change. I am running a PyTorch 1.14.0a0 development build with CUDA 12 on Ubuntu 20.04 and NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

symptoms_visible: My NeighborLoader GCN takes about 0.84 seconds per epoch in eager mode, while torch.compile is slower and emits cache-size-limit warnings as batch tensor sizes and strides change.
N0.label: N0 dynamic NeighborLoader compile performance reported

symptoms_visible: With dynamic=True, the compiled training run stops with a traceback containing 'TypeError: unhashable type: SymInt' while Inductor processes symbolic tensor sizes.
N1.label: N1 dynamic mode traceback collected

symptoms_visible: With dynamic=True, the compiled training run still stops with the SymInt traceback; the benchmark performs backward and an optimizer step.
N2.label: N2 training workload confirmed

symptoms_visible: After building the suggested training-support branch, eager mode runs, but the compiled model terminates with 'Segmentation fault (core dumped)'.
N2_x.label: N2_x training patch branch segfault aftermath

symptoms_visible: After rebuilding with the suggested branch and a current Triton source build, dynamic=True still fails: Tensor.size receives a SymInt where it expects an integer dimension.
N3_x.label: N3_x current Triton still fails dynamic compilation

symptoms_visible: With the suggested dynamic-shape configuration hack applied, the run gets as far as loss.backward(), then fails because an integer input has no '_has_symbolic_sizes_strides' attribute.
N4_x.label: N4_x configuration hack exposes backward failure

symptoms_visible: With current PyTorch, Triton, PyG and pyg-lib sources in April, the Inductor run completes, but averages about 1.08 seconds per epoch versus about 0.83 seconds in eager mode and warns that split reduction could not be used with dynamic shapes.
N5_x.label: N5_x correctness restored but performance still behind

symptoms_visible: After updating the stack and rerunning my NeighborLoader GCN benchmark, torch.compile completes training and is about 20% faster than eager mode.
N_terminal.label: terminal reporter observes NeighborLoader speedup

question_patterns: Can you rerun the NeighborLoader benchmark with dynamic=True and paste the raw result?
What happens if you explicitly enable dynamic shapes for torch.compile?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With dynamic=True, eager averages 0.7234251340230305 seconds per epoch, but the compiled run crashes. The traceback starts with `TypeError: unhashable type: 'SymInt'` and reaches Inductor while converting symbolic example sizes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: With dynamic=True the benchmark completes repeatedly and is faster than eager, with no symbolic-shape traceback.
The same SymInt traceback occurs, but eager averages 0.75 seconds per epoch instead.

edges.comment: Reporter c1 on the reporter's original environment: explicit dynamic mode changes the initial slowdown/recompilation report into a reproducible symbolic-shape compilation failure. The answer preserves the raw traceback rather than assigning a compiler root cause.

question_patterns: Is this benchmark training the model, including backward?
Does the reproducer call loss.backward rather than only running inference?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, this is training. The epoch runs the model, computes the loss, calls backward, and steps the optimizer.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No, it is inference-only and never calls backward.

edges.comment: Participant1 c2 first asked whether the reporter's benchmark was training. This clarification is separated from the subsequent branch recommendation so the newly supplied fact is available before a solution depends on it.

solution.intent: Build and test the then-proposed training-support branch to see whether its AOTAutograd changes allow this dynamic training workload to compile.
solution.concrete_example: Rebuild PyTorch from the linked training-support branch and rerun the same training script.

edges.comment: Participant1 c2 suggested the branch after learning this was training; reporter c3 built it on the reporter's system and got a segmentation fault. This was a real attempted fix and therefore lands on a persistent aftermath state.

question_patterns: Which Triton backend and source revision is this build using?
Can you determine whether the container has the older or current Triton backend?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I initially was not sure how to check because I was just using torch.compile in our February container. After checking with a colleague, I confirmed that container still used the old Triton backend; it built the Triton revision pinned by PyTorch at the start of February.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The segfault reproduces on a clean build using the current Triton backend and current PyTorch main without the proposed branch.
The container uses the same old backend, but its pinned revision is a few days newer.

solution.intent: Replace the old Triton backend with a current source build while retaining the training-support branch, then rerun with dynamic=True.
solution.concrete_example: Build the suggested PyTorch branch, install the latest Triton source build, and rerun the script with dynamic=True.

edges.comment: Participant1 c4 asked which backend was in use; reporter c5-c7 established that the February container used the old backend and rebuilt with current Triton. Reporter c9 then supplied the dynamic=True size(SymInt) failure from that new build. Updating Triton alone did not solve the reporter's dynamic training failure.

solution.intent: Temporarily force integer specialization inside the dynamic-shape context to bypass the size(SymInt) failure and unblock the training workload.
solution.concrete_example: Patch the dynamic-shape context so specialize_int_float is enabled, rebuild, and rerun the NeighborLoader training benchmark.

edges.comment: Participant1 c10-c11 supplied the configuration patch as a hack rather than a real fix. Reporter c14-c16 tested it together with the earlier branch and reached a different backward-compiler exception, so it did not unblock end-to-end training.

solution.intent: Move off the temporary patches and retest on current PyTorch, Triton, PyG and pyg-lib sources after the intervening dynamic-shape and compiler corrections.
solution.concrete_example: Build current PyTorch and Triton, update PyG and pyg-lib, and run the original dynamic NeighborLoader training script without relying on the earlier one-line specialization hack.

edges.comment: Engineering c23-c30 identified and fixed several successive failures, including missing inputs, split-reduction failures, insufficient backward guards, overspecialization and a PyG inspector graph break. Reporter c43 then tested current April sources: Inductor completed but was still slower than eager. Thus that April update solved correctness but was falsified as a complete performance resolution.

solution.intent: Use a current stack containing the accumulated dynamic-shape compiler corrections, evaluate the actual NeighborLoader training workload with sound CUDA timing, and require the reporter to confirm a real eager-versus-compiled improvement before declaring resolution.
solution.concrete_example: Update PyTorch, Triton and PyG together, rerun the same NeighborLoader GCN training benchmark with dynamic compilation, synchronize CUDA at timing boundaries, and compare warmed-up eager and compiled epochs. Do not rely on the old training branch or specialization hack; the reporter's later run observed about a 20% speedup.
solution.inference_hint: The thread does not establish one isolated regressing commit or one patch as the complete answer. Engineers successively identified symbolic-integer handling failures, backward guard problems, overspecialization, split-reduction limitations and graph breaks. They also found that synchronization between forward and backward could exaggerate benchmark speedups. Those conclusions are engineer-side interpretation; the reporter's terminal evidence is only that the later current-stack NeighborLoader run completed and produced about a 20% speedup.

edges.comment: Participant1 c40 and c54 raised the missing-CUDA-synchronization and benchmark-methodology concerns and quantified the relatively small dynamic-shape gain in a standardized benchmark. Reporter c55-c57 returned to the original NeighborLoader workload and personally reported a 20% torch.compile speedup. This is the affected reporter's own terminal verification, not the separate static benchmark results posted by other participants.

satisfaction_conditions: Must diagnose this as a sequence of dynamic-shape compiler correctness and performance problems affecting NeighborLoader training, including symbolic-size handling, backward guards or specialization, and dynamic reduction or graph-break overhead; it must not be reduced to the initial cache-size warning alone.
The recommendation must use a current PyTorch, Triton and PyG stack containing the accumulated corrections and must validate the original dynamic NeighborLoader training workload.
Performance claims must use sound CUDA timing with synchronization at timing boundaries because the thread established that synchronization placement could inflate apparent compiled speedups.

Must not present the old training-support branch, merely switching Triton backends, or enabling integer specialization as the final fix: each was tried in the reporter's chain and still crashed or failed during backward.
Must not treat the April build that merely completed at 1.08 seconds versus 0.83 seconds eager as a performance resolution.
Must require affected-reporter verification before declaring resolution; the terminal evidence is the reporter's later observation of about a 20% speedup on the NeighborLoader benchmark.

persona_hint.experience_level: Advanced ML infrastructure user comfortable building PyTorch and Triton from source, patching compiler configuration, running PyG training benchmarks, and supplying full tracebacks, but reliant on compiler maintainers to interpret symbolic-shape and Inductor internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, cooperative and deadline-oriented; posts raw timings and tracebacks, corrects earlier misunderstandings explicitly, follows build instructions, and repeatedly asks for practical progress on end-to-end NeighborLoader performance.
